questions.q: What does it mean that qubit parameters 'drift' over time?
options: Properties like resonant frequency, coherence times, and gate error rates change measurably over timescales of minutes to days, rather than staying fixed after a single characterization
Qubits physically move location inside the dilution refrigerator
Drift only refers to software bugs in the control electronics, not physical qubit behavior
Drift means the number of qubits on a chip changes unexpectedly
questions.explain: Drift refers to qubit parameters themselves changing over time due to physical causes, which is why a calibration done at one point can already be stale a few hours or days later.

questions.q: Which of these is a real physical source of qubit drift described in the lesson?
options: Two-level system (TLS) defects in the dielectric materials a qubit is built from, which can shift their own state over time and change how they couple to the qubit
Scheduled software updates to the classical control FPGA
The qubit's gate count exceeding a fixed maximum per day
A deliberate randomization process providers apply to discourage overuse of popular qubits
questions.explain: Microscopic material defects in a qubit's dielectric layers can behave like tiny two-level quantum systems that interact with the qubit and change their coupling over time -- one of several real physical sources of drift, alongside thermal fluctuations and flux noise.

questions.q: What does a periodic recalibration job actually do?
options: It re-measures key qubit parameters (like resonant frequency) and re-tunes control pulses accordingly, then updates the error-rate numbers the provider publishes
It physically replaces the qubit chip with a new one
It permanently eliminates all future drift for that device
It only runs once, at initial device installation, and never again
questions.explain: Recalibration is an automated routine that re-measures and re-tunes qubit parameters on an ongoing basis -- it doesn't eliminate drift, it bounds it, and it costs machine time that isn't spent running user circuits.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe a device's published fidelity/error-rate number as a 'snapshot' rather than a permanent spec?
options: Because the number reflects the most recent calibration run, and actual performance by the time a job runs could differ depending on how much drift has occurred since then
Because providers update published numbers purely for marketing purposes with no connection to actual measurements
Because fidelity numbers are only estimates that have never been physically measured on real hardware
Because every device on a given platform always reports the exact same fixed number
questions.explain: A published error rate is tied to the calibration run that produced it; drift since that measurement means real performance at job-submission time could be better or worse than the published snapshot.

questions.q: According to the lesson's honesty framing, why should calibration drift NOT be treated as an already-solved background process?
options: Recalibration itself has real costs (it uses machine time instead of running circuits), can't outrun drift faster than its own cadence, and only bounds run-to-run variability rather than eliminating it
Because no provider currently performs any recalibration at all
Because recalibration always makes error rates worse, never better
Because drift has been fully eliminated through newer qubit fabrication techniques as of recent years
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that recalibration is ongoing operational work with real limits -- it reduces but doesn't remove variability, and workloads with tight error budgets may need to check calibration data close to runtime rather than trusting it as permanently solved.
